claim: The expression of eukaryotic genes relies on the precise 3'-terminal cleavage and polyadenylation of newly synthesized pre-mRNA transcripts.
source: The expression of eukaryotic genes relies on the precise 3'-terminal cleavage and polyadenylation of newly synthesized pre-mRNA transcripts.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about eukaryotic gene expression.

claim: Defects in pre-mRNA cleavage and polyadenylation processes have been associated with various diseases, including cancer.
source: Defects in these processes have been associated with various diseases, including cancer.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Cancer-focused sequencing studies have identified numerous driver mutations in protein-coding sequences.
source: While cancer-focused sequencing studies have identified numerous driver mutations in protein-coding sequences, noncoding drivers – particularly those affecting the cis-elements required for pre-mRNA cleavage and polyadenylation – have received less attention.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium, 2020.

claim: Noncoding drivers affecting cis-elements required for pre-mRNA cleavage and polyadenylation have received less attention than protein-coding mutations.
source: While cancer-focused sequencing studies have identified numerous driver mutations in protein-coding sequences, noncoding drivers – particularly those affecting the cis-elements required for pre-mRNA cleavage and polyadenylation – have received less attention.
evidence: This is an inference based on the literature review presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a striking enrichment of cancer-specific somatic mutations that disrupt strong and evolutionarily conserved cleavage and polyadenylation signals within tumour suppressor genes.
source: We found a striking enrichment of cancer-specific somatic mutations that disrupt strong and evolutionarily conserved cleavage and polyadenylation signals within tumour suppressor genes.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis of the PCAWG dataset presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations disrupting cleavage and polyadenylation signals have a profound capacity to downregulate the expression of tumour suppressor genes.
source: Further bioinformatics and experimental analyses conducted as a part of our study suggest that these mutations have a profound capacity to downregulate the expression of tumour suppressor genes.
evidence: This is supported by both bioinformatics and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Somatic mutations disrupting cleavage and polyadenylation signals represent a novel class of noncoding somatic mutations with significant potential to drive cancer progression.
source: Thus, this work uncovers a novel class of noncoding somatic mutations with significant potential to drive cancer progression.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most eukaryotic mRNAs are modified by the addition of a 5'-terminal 7-methylguanosine cap, splicing of intronic sequences, and 3'-terminal cleavage and polyadenylation.
source: Most eukaryotic mRNAs are modified by the addition of a 5'-terminal 7-methylguanosine cap, splicing of intronic sequences, and 3'-terminal cleavage and polyadenylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic mRNA processing.

claim: The cleavage and polyadenylation reactions are tightly coupled with transcription termination and the release of newly synthesized transcripts from RNA polymerase II.
source: The cleavage and polyadenylation reactions are tightly coupled with transcription termination and the release of newly synthesized transcripts from RNA polymerase II.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Precise cleavage and polyadenylation are critical for the production of mature mRNAs.
source: Therefore, precise cleavage and polyadenylation are critical for the production of mature mRNAs.
evidence: This is an inference from the coupling of cleavage/polyadenylation with transcription termination.

claim: Cleavage and polyadenylation reactions require a co-transcriptional assembly of a multisubunit protein complex at the corresponding cis-regulatory sequences near the pre-mRNA cleavage site.
source: Mechanistically, these reactions require a co-transcriptional assembly of a multisubunit protein complex at the corresponding cis-regulatory sequences near the pre-mRNA cleavage site (CS) (Tian and Manley, 2017; Neve et al., 2017; Shi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The polyadenylation signal (PAS) is a key cis-element guiding the assembly of the cleavage and polyadenylation machinery.
source: A key cis-element guiding the assembly of the cleavage and polyadenylation machinery is the polyadenylation signal (PAS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pre-mRNA processing.

claim: The most common PAS sequences in mammals are AATAAA and ATTAAA hexamers.
source: The most common PAS sequences in mammals are AATAAA and ATTAAA hexamers, although their single nucleotide-substituted variants may function in some cases (Proudfoot, 1991; Beaudoing et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Single nucleotide-substituted variants of AATAAA and ATTAAA may function as polyadenylation signals in some cases.
source: The most common PAS sequences in mammals are AATAAA and ATTAAA hexamers, although their single nucleotide-substituted variants may function in some cases (Proudfoot, 1991; Beaudoing et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Alternative cleavage/polyadenylation has been proposed to modulate the expression of oncogenes and tumour suppressors in different types of cancer.
source: For example, alternative cleavage/polyadenylation has been proposed to modulate the expression of oncogenes and tumour suppressors in different types of cancer (Mayr and Bartel, 2009; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Germline mutations affecting polyadenylation signals can play a role in genetic disorders.
source: Germline mutations affecting polyadenylation signals can play a role in genetic disorders (Higgs et al., 1983; Bogard et al., 2019; Bennett et al., 2001) and increase cancer susceptibility (Stacey et al., 2011; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Germline mutations affecting polyadenylation signals can increase cancer susceptibility.
source: Germline mutations affecting polyadenylation signals can play a role in genetic disorders (Higgs et al., 1983; Bogard et al., 2019; Bennett et al., 2001) and increase cancer susceptibility (Stacey et al., 2011; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The role of somatic mutations affecting polyadenylation signals has been investigated for individual genes in a limited number of tumour samples.
source: Notably, although the role of somatic mutations affecting polyadenylation signals has been investigated for individual genes in a limited number of tumour samples (Wiestner et al., 2007; Shlien et al., 2016), a systematic characterisation of the role of this type of mutation in cancer has not been carried out.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A systematic characterisation of the role of somatic mutations affecting polyadenylation signals in cancer has not been carried out prior to this study.
source: Notably, although the role of somatic mutations affecting polyadenylation signals has been investigated for individual genes in a limited number of tumour samples (Wiestner et al., 2007; Shlien et al., 2016), a systematic characterisation of the role of this type of mutation in cancer has not been carried out.
evidence: This is an inference based on literature review.

claim: Large-scale genome sequencing studies have identified numerous cancer driver and driver-like mutations within protein-coding sequences.
source: Large-scale genome sequencing studies have identified numerous cancer driver and driver-like mutations within protein-coding sequences (ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the PCAWG consortium.

claim: Cancer driver mutations have been mapped to noncoding regions, with existing research primarily focused on promoters, enhancers, and splicing signals rather than sequences regulating pre-mRNA cleavage and polyadenylation.
source: Such mutations have also been mapped to noncoding regions; however, existing research has primarily focused on promoters, enhancers, and splicing signals (Cao et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Sherman et al., 2022; Rheinbay et al., 2020; Calabrese et al., 2020), rather than sequences regulating pre-mRNA cleavage and polyadenylation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: paSNVs predicted to have a strong impact on cleavage/polyadenylation are often situated immediately upstream of a cleavage site.
source: As expected, paSNVs predicted to have a strong impact on cleavage/polyadenylation were often situated immediately upstream of a CS, with most of them affecting AWTAAA hexamers (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Most paSNVs with strong impact on cleavage/polyadenylation affect AWTAAA hexamers.
source: As expected, paSNVs predicted to have a strong impact on cleavage/polyadenylation were often situated immediately upstream of a CS, with most of them affecting AWTAAA hexamers (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The presence of AATAAA or ATTAAA in polyadenylation signals is associated with a high APARENT2 score.
source: Furthermore, the presence of AATAAA or ATTAAA in polyadenylation signals tended to be associated with a high APARENT2 score (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and the loss or gain of AATAAA led to a significantly stronger decrease or increase in the score, respectively, compared to other mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The loss or gain of AATAAA leads to a significantly stronger decrease or increase in the APARENT2 score, respectively, compared to other mutations.
source: Furthermore, the presence of AATAAA or ATTAAA in polyadenylation signals tended to be associated with a high APARENT2 score (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and the loss or gain of AATAAA led to a significantly stronger decrease or increase in the score, respectively, compared to other mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is pronounced negative selection against DOWN-paSNVs in the normal population.
source: Consistent with the earlier studies (Linder et al., 2022; Kainov et al., 2016; Findlay et al., 2022), we observed a pronounced negative selection against the DOWN-paSNVs in the Normal dataset (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D, and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: DOWN-paSNVs show significantly decreased allele frequencies compared to BG-paSNVs in the normal population.
source: This category showed significantly decreased allele frequencies in comparison to the BG-paSNVs and was enriched for singletons (unique variants in the analysed dataset).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DOWN-paSNVs are enriched for singletons in the normal population.
source: This category showed significantly decreased allele frequencies in comparison to the BG-paSNVs and was enriched for singletons (unique variants in the analysed dataset).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cancer somatic mutations have a stronger effect on polyadenylation efficiency compared to normal population variants in both UP- and DOWN-paSNV groups.
source: Notably, a comparison of the Normal and Cancer datasets showed that cancer somatic mutations, on average, had a stronger effect on the polyadenylation efficiency in both the UP- and DOWN-paSNV groups (Figure 1B; LOR sample variance 0.115 in cancer vs 0.0876 in normal).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and statistical comparison of LOR sample variance.

claim: DOWN-paSNVs are significantly enriched in cancer compared to the normal population.
source: DOWN-paSNVs were significantly enriched in cancer compared to the normal population data (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mutations disrupting AWTAAA hexamers in 3'UTRs tend to occur near annotated cleavage sites in cancer.
source: We also observed that mutations disrupting AWTAAA hexamers in 3'UTRs tended to occur near annotated cleavage sites in cancer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cancer-specific DOWN-paSNVs affect cleavage/polyadenylation signals with higher APARENT2 scores compared to normal population variants.
source: Interestingly, cancer-specific DOWN-paSNVs affected cleavage/polyadenylation signals with higher APARENT2 scores (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DOWN-paSNVs affect more evolutionarily conserved sequences in cancer compared to the normal population.
source: Furthermore, DOWN-paSNVs tended to affect more evolutionarily conserved sequences in the Cancer dataset compared to the Normal control (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1614 distinct cancer somatic DOWN-paSNVs were identified affecting 1570 cleavage/polyadenylation events in 1460 genes in 602 tumours.
source: In total, we identified 1614 distinct cancer somatic DOWN-paSNVs affecting 1570 cleavage/polyadenylation events in 1460 genes in 602 tumours, i.e., 22.7% of all tumour samples in PCAWG (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the bioinformatics analysis.

claim: DOWN-paSNVs were found in 22.7% of all tumour samples in PCAWG.
source: In total, we identified 1614 distinct cancer somatic DOWN-paSNVs affecting 1570 cleavage/polyadenylation events in 1460 genes in 602 tumours, i.e., 22.7% of all tumour samples in PCAWG (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the bioinformatics analysis.

claim: Nearly half of the DOWN-paSNVs originated from colorectal adenocarcinoma.
source: Notably, nearly half of the DOWN-paSNVs originated from colorectal adenocarcinoma, with the remaining mutations distributed across a wide range of other cancer types (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: DOWN-paSNVs show a remarkable over-representation in tumour suppressor genes.
source: This revealed a remarkable over-representation of the DOWN-paSNVs in tumour suppressor genes, with the magnitude of this effect being greater than the corresponding enrichment of nonsense mutations (SNVs creating a premature translation termination codon) (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The enrichment of DOWN-paSNVs in tumour suppressor genes is greater than the enrichment of nonsense mutations.
source: This revealed a remarkable over-representation of the DOWN-paSNVs in tumour suppressor genes, with the magnitude of this effect being greater than the corresponding enrichment of nonsense mutations (SNVs creating a premature translation termination codon) (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DOWN-paSNVs are not enriched in oncogenes.
source: Notably, DOWN-paSNVs were not enriched in the oncogenes (Figure 3C), in line with the disruptive nature of such mutations under normal conditions (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Oncogenes show enrichment for UP-paSNVs but not tumour suppressors.
source: Conversely, oncogenes but not tumour suppressors showed some enrichment for UP-paSNVs (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DOWN-paSNVs affect 38 tumour suppressor genes, representing 14.3% of all genes in this category in the Census dataset.
source: Overall, DOWN-paSNVs were found to affect 38 tumour suppressor genes, i.e., 14.3% of all genes in this category in the Census dataset.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the bioinformatics analysis.

claim: In several cases, including LRP1B and FOXO1, the same polyadenylation signal was disrupted by the same or different mutations in more than one sample.
source: In several cases, including LRP1B and FOXO1, which are known to act as tumour suppressors in certain cancers, the same signal/polyadenylation signal was disrupted by the same or different mutations in more than one sample (see columns Mut_Recurrence and Signal_Recurrence in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: LRP1B and FOXO1 are known to act as tumour suppressors in certain cancers.
source: In several cases, including LRP1B and FOXO1, which are known to act as tumour suppressors in certain cancers, the same signal/polyadenylation signal was disrupted by the same or different mutations in more than one sample (see columns Mut_Recurrence and Signal_Recurrence in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about these genes.

claim: Genes with DOWN-paSNVs are significantly enriched for apoptosis-related functions.
source: Consistent with tumour suppressors being a major target of DOWN-paSNVs, genes with this type of mutations were significantly enriched for apoptosis-related functions (Figure 3D; e.g. tumour suppressors CASP9 or FHIT).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Genes with DOWN-paSNVs show enrichment of proteins interacting with the ubiquitination pathway.
source: We also detected the enrichment of proteins interacting with the ubiquitination pathway (Figure 3D, E; e.g. tumour suppressors SMAD2, APC, and AXIN1).
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: DOWN-paSNV events show a significantly higher observed-to-expected mutation rate in cancer compared to the BG-paSNV group according to DigDriver analysis.
source: This analysis revealed a significantly higher observed-to-expected mutation rate for DOWN-paSNV events in cancer compared to the BG-paSNV group (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by DigDriver analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: DOWN-paSNVs are enriched in tumour suppressor genes according to DigDriver analysis, consistent with positive selection for these events in cancer.
source: DOWN-paSNVs tended to be enriched in tumour suppressor genes, consistent with positive selection for these events in cancer (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by DigDriver analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No enrichment of DOWN-paSNVs was detected in oncogenes according to DigDriver analysis.
source: No such enrichment was detected in oncogenes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by DigDriver analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Tumour suppressor 3'UTRs are characterized by stronger cleavage/polyadenylation signals compared to oncogenes and non-cancer genes.
source: Of note, our analysis of wild-type sequences showed that tumour suppressor 3'UTRs are characterized by stronger cleavage/polyadenylation signals compared to oncogenes and non-cancer genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Tumour suppressors associated with hallmarks of cancer have stronger cleavage/polyadenylation signals than other tumour suppressor genes.
source: Moreover, tumour suppressors associated with hallmarks of cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011) in the Census dataset had stronger cleavage/polyadenylation signals than the rest of tumour suppressor genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: DOWN-paSNV-containing tumour suppressors show a markedly increased incidence of damaging non-synonymous mutations in the same tumour compared to the BG-paSNV control.
source: DOWN-paSNV-containing tumour suppressors showed a markedly increased incidence of such additional somatic mutations in the same tumour compared to the BG-paSNV control (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The overall frequency of damaging non-synonymous mutations in tumour suppressors affected by DOWN-paSNVs is significantly higher than in the DOWN-paSNV-negative tumour suppressor group.
source: Furthermore, the overall frequency of damaging non-synonymous mutations in tumour suppressors affected by DOWN-paSNVs in at least one sample was significantly higher than in the DOWN-paSNV-negative tumour suppressor group (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Increased copy number is 4.1 times more common in the PCAWG data compared to allele loss.
source: The analysis of allele copy number variation (CNV) showed that increased copy number was 4.1 times more common in the PCAWG data compared to allele loss.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from CNV analysis.

claim: The incidence of copy number increase is substantially lower in the DOWN-paSNV group compared to the BG-paSNV control.
source: However, the incidence of copy number increase was substantially lower in the DOWN-paSNV group compared to the BG-paSNV control (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is negative selection against duplications of genes affected by DOWN-paSNVs in cancer.
source: This points to a negative selection against duplications of genes affected by DOWN-paSNVs in cancer.
evidence: This is an inference from the CNV data.

claim: Seven tumour suppressor genes (CASP9, NDRG1, XPA, TSC1, ETV6, ISY1, and SMAD2) containing DOWN-paSNVs and no other damaging mutations in specific cancer samples were detectably expressed in colorectal adenocarcinoma.
source: We shortlisted detectably expressed tumour suppressors that contained DOWN-paSNVs and no other damaging mutations in specific cancer samples, and were wild-type in other samples. Seven genes passing these filters were involved in various aspects of tumour biology, including cell survival and DNA repair (CASP9, NDRG1, and XPA), mTOR signalling (TSC1), and transcription and RNA processing (ETV6, ISY1, and SMAD2).
evidence: This is based on filtering of gene expression data from colorectal adenocarcinoma samples.

claim: There is a significant bias towards downregulation in samples containing DOWN-paSNVs compared to wild-type controls for the aggregated tumour suppressor set.
source: Plotting pairwise gene-specific expression differences for the aggregated tumour suppressor set, we observed a significant bias towards downregulation in the samples containing DOWN-paSNVs compared to the wild-type controls (Figure 5A; median downregulation of 1.25-fold).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The median downregulation for the aggregated tumour suppressor set containing DOWN-paSNVs is 1.25-fold.
source: Plotting pairwise gene-specific expression differences for the aggregated tumour suppressor set, we observed a significant bias towards downregulation in the samples containing DOWN-paSNVs compared to the wild-type controls (Figure 5A; median downregulation of 1.25-fold).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from gene expression analysis.

claim: All seven individual tumour suppressor genes show negative biases in expression, with median downregulation values ranging from 1.1- to 3.2-fold.
source: Remarkably, similar negative biases were detected for all seven individual genes, with median downregulation values ranging from 1.1- to 3.2-fold (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A somatic mutation in the XPA gene alters the canonical AATAAA PAS hexamer to GATAAA near the terminal cleavage site.
source: The XPA mutation identified by our bioinformatics analyses alters the canonical AATAAA PAS hexamer to GATAAA near the terminal CS and significantly reduces the APARENT2 score (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The XPA mutation significantly reduces the APARENT2 score.
source: The XPA mutation identified by our bioinformatics analyses alters the canonical AATAAA PAS hexamer to GATAAA near the terminal CS and significantly reduces the APARENT2 score (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by APARENT2 analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The XPA DOWN-paSNV causes a significant decrease in cleavage/polyadenylation efficiency as measured by RT-qPCR.
source: An RT-qPCR assay measuring the efficiency of cleavage/polyadenylation as a ratio between the CS-read-through and CS-upstream signals revealed a significant decrease in cleavage/polyadenylation efficiency in response to the XPA DOWN-paSNV (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The XPA mutation significantly reduces luciferase protein production compared to the wild-type control.
source: Following the transfection of HCT-116 cells, we detected a significantly reduced production of luciferase protein from the mutant construct compared to the wild-type control (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: XPA has been shown to promote apoptosis in response to DNA damage, in addition to its role in nucleotide excision repair.
source: This gene has been shown to promote apoptosis in response to DNA damage, in addition to its role in nucleotide excision repair (Deng et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Downregulation of XPA has been associated with decreased patient survival in colorectal cancer.
source: Moreover, downregulation of XPA has been associated with decreased patient survival in colorectal cancer (Feng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mutations disrupting polyadenylation signals are likely deleterious as they are subjected to strong negative selection in the normal population.
source: Our analyses confirm that germline SNVs disrupting PAS are likely deleterious, as they are subjected to strong negative selection in the normal population (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Somatic mutations affecting polyadenylation signals in cancer are more prevalent than in the normal population.
source: Intriguingly, we found that somatic mutations affecting such cis-elements in cancer are more prevalent, tend to occur near stronger CSs, and target more evolutionarily conserved PAS hexamers (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Somatic mutations affecting polyadenylation signals in cancer tend to occur near stronger cleavage sites.
source: Intriguingly, we found that somatic mutations affecting such cis-elements in cancer are more prevalent, tend to occur near stronger CSs, and target more evolutionarily conserved PAS hexamers (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Somatic mutations affecting polyadenylation signals in cancer target more evolutionarily conserved PAS hexamers.
source: Intriguingly, we found that somatic mutations affecting such cis-elements in cancer are more prevalent, tend to occur near stronger CSs, and target more evolutionarily conserved PAS hexamers (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cancer somatic SNVs disrupt PAS sequences in tumour suppressor genes with a similar enrichment pattern to nonsense mutations.
source: Importantly, these cancer somatic SNVs disrupt PAS sequences in tumour suppressor genes with a similar enrichment pattern to well-known deleterious SNVs in protein-coding regions, such as nonsense mutations (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Wild-type tumour suppressors have stronger cleavage/polyadenylation signals than other groups of genes.
source: Additionally, wild-type tumour suppressors have stronger cleavage/polyadenylation signals than other groups of genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), pointing to the importance of the corresponding steps of pre-mRNA processing for their expression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The stronger cleavage/polyadenylation signals in tumour suppressors point to the importance of pre-mRNA processing for their expression.
source: Additionally, wild-type tumour suppressors have stronger cleavage/polyadenylation signals than other groups of genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), pointing to the importance of the corresponding steps of pre-mRNA processing for their expression.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation about signal strength.

claim: Tumour suppressors with disrupted cleavage/polyadenylation signals are more likely to acquire other damaging somatic mutations in the same tumour.
source: Consistent with the two-hit hypothesis (Knudson, 1971), we found that tumour suppressors with disrupted cleavage/polyadenylation signals (i.e. containing DOWN-paSNVs) are more likely to acquire other damaging somatic mutations in the same tumour (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D, and is consistent with the two-hit hypothesis.

claim: Tumour suppressors containing only DOWN-paSNVs are consistently expressed at lower levels compared to their wild-type counterparts.
source: Indeed, tumour suppressors containing only DOWN-paSNVs are consistently expressed at lower levels compared to their wild-type counterparts (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Partial inactivation of many tumour suppressors can be sufficient to promote tumorigenesis.
source: Moreover, it is currently thought that partial inactivation of many tumour suppressors can be sufficient to promote tumorigenesis (Berger et al., 2011; Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A cancer-specific single-nucleotide mutation disrupting the PAS hexamer in XPA is sufficient to block pre-mRNA cleavage/polyadenylation.
source: Using the tumour suppressor gene XPA as an example, we directly show that a cancer-specific single-nucleotide mutation disrupting the PAS hexamer is sufficient to block pre-mRNA cleavage/polyadenylation and dampen the expression of mature mRNA (Figure 5C, E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and E.

claim: A cancer-specific single-nucleotide mutation disrupting the PAS hexamer in XPA dampens the expression of mature mRNA.
source: Using the tumour suppressor gene XPA as an example, we directly show that a cancer-specific single-nucleotide mutation disrupting the PAS hexamer is sufficient to block pre-mRNA cleavage/polyadenylation and dampen the expression of mature mRNA (Figure 5C, E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and E.

claim: SNVs targeting polyadenylation signals can have a profound effect on gene expression in cancer.
source: These results support our bioinformatics analyses and argue that SNVs targeting polyadenylation signals can have a profound effect on gene expression in cancer.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Germline SNVs affecting PAS have similar gene expression effects as shown in previous reports.
source: Our data are also consistent with previous reports showing similar gene expression effects of PAS-specific germline SNVs (Higgs et al., 1983; Bennett et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mutation of cleavage/polyadenylation signals is expected to lead to the appearance of abnormal read-through transcripts that may be destabilized by RNA quality control mechanisms.
source: It is expected that mutation of cleavage/polyadenylation signals should lead to the appearance of abnormal read-through transcripts that may be destabilized by either nuclear or cytoplasmic RNA quality control mechanisms (Bresson and Tollervey, 2018).
evidence: This is speculation based on known RNA quality control mechanisms.

claim: A decrease in cleavage/polyadenylation activity might dampen transcription initiation, as these two processes are known to be interconnected.
source: Alternatively, a decrease in cleavage/polyadenylation activity might dampen transcription initiation, as these two processes are known to be interconnected (Mapendano et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation based on known interconnection between processes.

claim: The genetic inactivation of cleavage and polyadenylation in tumour suppressor genes constitutes a prevalent, yet previously overlooked category of somatic cancer mutations with driver properties.
source: In conclusion, our study reveals that the genetic inactivation of cleavage and polyadenylation in tumour suppressor genes constitutes a prevalent, yet previously overlooked category of somatic cancer mutations with driver properties.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the data presented.

claim: The findings emphasize the importance of pre-mRNA processing in the biology of cancer.
source: These findings emphasize the importance of pre-mRNA processing in the biology of cancer and underscore the need for improved functional annotation of single nucleotide variants in noncoding regions of the human genome.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings of the study.

claim: There is a need for improved functional annotation of single nucleotide variants in noncoding regions of the human genome.
source: These findings emphasize the importance of pre-mRNA processing in the biology of cancer and underscore the need for improved functional annotation of single nucleotide variants in noncoding regions of the human genome.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings of the study.

claim: APARENT2 neural network model infers changes in cleavage/polyadenylation efficiency more accurately than earlier approaches.
source: For each paSNV, we calculated the change in cleavage/polyadenylation efficiency using the APARENT2 neural network model, which has been shown to infer this statistic more accurately than earlier approaches (Linder et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the APARENT2 publication.

claim: UP-paSNVs are defined as events with a ≥1 increase in the APARENT2 score and creating an AWTAAA hexamer.
source: We then categorized all paSNVs into three groups: (1) upregulating cleavage/polyadenylation (UP-paSNVs), defined as events with a ≥1 increase in the APARENT2 score (log odds ratio, or LOR) and creating an AWTAAA hexamer
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: DOWN-paSNVs are defined as events with LOR≤–1 and disrupting an AWTAAA hexamer.
source: (2) downregulating cleavage/polyadenylation (DOWN-paSNVs; LOR≤–1 and disrupting an AWTAAA)
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: BG-paSNVs are the remaining annotated cleavage position-adjacent paSNVs that serve as a background control.
source: and (3) the remaining annotated cleavage position-adjacent paSNVs (Figure 1B). The latter group served as a background control (BG-paSNVs) in our subsequent analyses.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: HCT-116 cells were confirmed to have characteristic morphology using light microscopy.
source: HCT-116 cells were purchased from ATCC (Cat# CCL-247), confirmed to have characteristic morphology using light microscopy (https://www.atcc.org/products/ccl-247#detailed-product-images), and tested negative for mycoplasma contamination using a LookOut Mycoplasma PCR Detection Kit (Sigma-Aldrich, cat# MP0035).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about cell line validation.

claim: HCT-116 cells tested negative for mycoplasma contamination.
source: HCT-116 cells were purchased from ATCC (Cat# CCL-247), confirmed to have characteristic morphology using light microscopy (https://www.atcc.org/products/ccl-247#detailed-product-images), and tested negative for mycoplasma contamination using a LookOut Mycoplasma PCR Detection Kit (Sigma-Aldrich, cat# MP0035).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about cell line validation.
